selected.title: CDP Developer Portal
selected.description: Launched and migrated users to a new self-serve logged-in developer portal built to serve solo developers, enterprises, and everyone in between.
body: ## Quick hits
- Two years as PM for the CDP Portal, from the V1 developer console through the V2 enterprise rebuild
- Grew V1 from ~2K to ~15K developers while onboarding 10 new API products, mostly onchain-native: Node, non-custodial wallets, onchain data APIs
- Nov 2025: shipped the Portal V2 MVP in private beta, with sandbox, as the launch surface for CDP's new enterprise payments products
- Jun 2026: shipped the fully unified Portal V2 to GA, migrated 17,000+ active CDP entities, and retired V1 on June 22, the date we committed to
- Monthly Payments Platform volume went from ~$5M (Oct 2025) to ~$30M (Jun 2026, GA) to ~$213M (Oct 2026)
{{gallery}}

I spent two years as the PM for the Coinbase Developer Platform portal. When I started, it was a console for individual developers: sign up, grab an API key, start building. By the time I handed it off, it was where fintechs, payment processors, and banks tested, integrated, and ran their business on Coinbase.
## The V1 years
Portal V1 was good at what it was built for. A developer could go from signup to a working key in a few minutes, and “projects” let one person keep a few experiments separate.

Over that stretch we onboarded 10 new API products into the portal, most of them onchain-native: Node, non-custodial wallets, onchain data APIs, and more. Each one needed its own place in the console, its own key flow, and its own getting-started path. The developer base grew from about 2,000 to about 15,000 along the way, and most of what I shipped was about keeping that loop fast as the product surface got wider: onboarding, key management, docs integration.
## Where V1 broke down
In 2025 CDP moved upmarket. The customers we wanted were enterprises using several CDP products at once: payments, custody, trading, stablecoins. V1 had no way to hold a company.
- **One human account per customer.** No organization, no roles, no way to give a finance teammate read-only access.

- **Inconsistent API keys.** Some products were on the shared CDP API key, others still had their own. A customer using several products had to know which was which and manage them in different places.
- **Two portals.** Enterprise payments lived in a separate experience. Two logins, two mental models.
- **No single view of money.** Custodial balances, payment methods, and onchain wallets were never on one screen.

- **No sandbox.** A large business will not integrate against production to find out how a flow works. Every evaluation turned into a hand-held process: calls to walk through the APIs, test credentials provisioned by engineers, demo environments built by hand. Sales could describe the product but could not let a prospect touch it.
Payments volume was about $5M a month in October 2025, and the portal was one of the main reasons enterprise deals were slow to land.
## Private beta: November 2025

We didn't wait for the full rebuild. In November 2025 we shipped a Portal V2 MVP to private beta, with sandbox from the start, and made it the home for CDP's new enterprise payments products. As each one came online, it landed in V2, not V1. That gave us real enterprise customers on the new model months before GA, and gave the payments teams somewhere to ship without waiting on the migration.
## GA: June 2026
GA was the fully unified portal. V1 and the separate payments experience folded into one.
- **New account model.** Organization, then Project, then Account. Users and role-based permissions sit on the organization, not on one person.
- **One key system.** Every product moved onto org-level CDP API keys, with project-scoped keys to limit a key to the part of the business it should touch.
- **Accounts tab.** Wallets grouped as custodial, self-custodial, and payment methods, so you can see where funds sit at a glance.

- **Activity tab.** A filter-driven table over 72 activity types across payments, trading, wallets, and stablecoins. Filters define both the rows and the columns, and any view can be turned into a report.

- **Sandbox mode across every product.** Sign up with an email and password, create a sandbox API key, flip the portal to sandbox mode, and start creating and managing sandbox resources. No contract, no KYB, no call with an engineer.

Sandbox was the hardest piece. Every product in the portal needed a sandbox version of its APIs and its data, so the work cut across several teams with their own roadmaps. We had to agree on what “sandbox” meant, how sandbox resources relate to live ones, and how a customer moves between the two without getting lost.
It ended up being much more than a test environment:
- **The front door.** Prospects got in, poked at the APIs, and built their integration against sandbox before the commercial conversation was done.
- **The demo.** Sales and solutions engineers used the portal in sandbox mode instead of slides.
- **Faster go-lives.** By the time a contract was signed, the customer often already had a working integration ready to flip to live.
## Shipping it without breaking anyone
- Migrated more than 17,000 active CDP entities to the new model while V1 kept serving traffic.
- Dogfooded internally, opened to customers, then shut V1 down on June 22, 2026, the date we committed to.
- Hit the launch goal: 100% of Portal and API traffic routing and authenticating through the new systems.
## What happened next

Three numbers tell the story: about $5M a month in October 2025 before the private beta, about $30M in June 2026 at GA, about $213M in October 2026. Once the portal stopped being the thing in the way, enterprises could evaluate, integrate, and operate on CDP the way they expected to. The teams behind that volume started in sandbox and now manage their accounts, keys, and transfers in Portal V2 every day.
## What I took from it
- **Ship the new surface early.** Getting the MVP into private beta seven months before GA meant new products never had to land in the old portal.
- **The account model is the product.** Everything that was hard in V1 was hard because the data model assumed one person.
- **A sandbox is a sales tool.** The fastest way to convince an enterprise is to let them try it without asking anyone.
- **A migration is a feature.** Most of the effort went into making the cutover invisible, and that was the right call.

selected.title: AI-Native Docs, with Mintlify
selected.description: Led a full overhaul of CDP's developer docs: rebuilt the information architecture, shipped AI-first features like one-click copy-to-LLM and an MCP server, and cut internal preview build times from 30 minutes to under one. Shipped in 6 weeks.
selected.linkLabel: Read my writeup on Coinbase's blog ↗
body: CDP's developer docs had grown organically for years: inconsistent information architecture, a slow internal preview loop, and no affordances for how developers actually use docs now (copy-pasting into LLMs, asking AI assistants directly).

I scoped a full overhaul in partnership with Mintlify: rebuilt the IA from scratch, consolidated hundreds of pages, and shipped a set of AI-native features: one-click copy-to-LLM for any code block, an MCP server so developers could query the docs from their AI tools, and better search. On the tooling side, we cut internal preview build times from 30 minutes to under one, so the docs team could actually iterate in real time.
Shipped in 6 weeks. I wrote up the full story (the ETH Denver research that kicked this off, what we learned, what I'd do differently) on Coinbase's blog, linked above.

projects.title: Ultimate Frisbee Jerseys
projects.description: Designed a full custom jersey kit for my club team, from concept sketches to production-ready print files.
body: Designed a complete custom jersey kit for my club ultimate frisbee team, both the home and away sets. Started from rough sketches, iterated through a few concepts based on team feedback, and ended up with production-ready vector files sent to the manufacturer.

The design had to work at small print sizes, hold up on dark and light colorways, and feel like something the team was actually excited to wear. We went through three rounds of revisions before locking it in.

projects.title: Social Media Graphics
projects.description: Created marketing & graphic design assets for NYU's Strategic Venture Society, an undergraduate VC club.
body: Served as the in-house designer for NYU's Strategic Venture Society, an undergraduate VC club focused on connecting students with the startup ecosystem.

Over two years I created the full range of visual assets: event promotion graphics, speaker announcement cards, LinkedIn and Instagram content, and pitch deck templates. Developed a consistent visual identity that carried across all touchpoints.

projects.title: Sustainability Proposal
projects.description: Wrote a feature on Olympic sustainability for NYU Stern's Corporate Action magazine, The Call.
body: Wrote a feature article on the sustainability challenges facing the Olympic Games for The Call, NYU Stern's Corporate Action magazine.

The piece examined how host cities have historically struggled with post-Games infrastructure costs and environmental footprint, and proposed a framework for evaluating future bids through a sustainability lens.
